newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Cousteau laid to rest in private burial.
newsitem.headline: France's Cousteau laid to rest in private burial.

text.p: French oceanographer Jacques-Yves Cousteau, who introduced the wonders of the sea to the world, was laid to rest on Thursday in a in the southwestern French town where he was born.
Cousteau was buried in the family plot in Saint-Andre-de-Cubzac, a town of 5,000 just outside the French wine capital Bordeaux.

Some 30 family members were joined at the funeral by several hundred admirers who gathered outside the cemetery wall to pay their last respects to the captain of the Calypso, the converted British minesweeper which took Cousteau to the far corners of the globe in search of knowledge and adventure.
Cousteau, who revealed the mysteries of the oceans in prize-winning films and books and campaigned around the world to protect the environment, died on June 25, aged 87.
A mass in his honour at the towering 12th-century Notre Dame Cathedral in central Paris on Monday drew thousands of mourners including French President Jacques Chirac.

A former navy officer who went on to become an explorer, ecologist, filmmaker and millionaire, he also was co-inventor in 1943 of diving gear that freed undersea explorers from heavy helmets, allowing them to float in the water as if in space.
Cousteau's widow Francine has pledged to pursue his projects after his death and was this week formally named head of the Cousteau Foundation.

She said her top priorities were to build a Calypso II to keep exploring the world as "a lookout to tomorrow's problems", and to start up a television channel called "The Human Voice" to record the culture and language of endangered peoples.
